name: AI Tools Every Entrepreneur Should Know
objectives: Given any AI tool, identify which of four business jobs it does: writing, design, documents and numbers, or meetings and notes, and check its job, cost and fit before adding it

chapters.name: Chapter 1: The main kinds of AI tools

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The AI tool map: four jobs, not four hundred apps
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Sort AI tools by the job they do for your business.
This lesson builds toward: Given any AI tool, you will identify which of four business jobs it does: writing, design, documents and numbers, or meetings and notes, and check its job, cost and fit before adding it.
Most AI tools a small business needs fall into four jobs. Writing and thinking: chat assistants like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini. Design: tools like Canva that make graphics, flyers and social images. Documents and numbers: AI built into Google Docs and Sheets or Microsoft Word and Excel. Meetings and notes: tools that record, transcribe and summarize.
Many tools now do more than one job. A chat assistant can also make an image or read a spreadsheet you upload. That is fine, but starting with one tool per job keeps things simple.
Before you add any new tool, ask: What job does it do? Do I already have a tool for that job? Is there a free plan? What happens to the data I put in?
Words to know:
- Chat assistant: an AI tool you talk to in a chat window, such as ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini.
- Transcribe: turn spoken words into written text.
Try it now: Write the four jobs on a page. Next to each, write any tool you already use for it (even a non-AI one). Leave blanks where you have none.
You can now sort AI tools into four business jobs and ask four questions before adding a new one.

check.q: Which job does a transcription tool do?
check.why: Transcription turns speech into notes, which is the meetings and notes job.

check.q: A new AI app promises to write social posts, but you already have a chat assistant that does it. What do you do?
options: Sign up for it at once
Skip it unless it does the job clearly better
check.why: One tool per job keeps things simple and avoids paying twice.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Chat assistants: picking one and using it well
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free chat assistant and use it for a real business writing job.
This lesson builds toward: Using the accounts your business already has, you will choose a free chat assistant and use it for a real business writing job, after comparing the same prompt in two assistants.
ChatGPT (chatgpt.com), Microsoft Copilot (copilot.microsoft.com) and Google Gemini (gemini.google.com) all have free versions. They all write, summarize, brainstorm and explain. Pick the one that fits the accounts you already use: Copilot if your business runs on Microsoft, Gemini if it runs on Google, or any of them if you are not sure.
Use the same three-part prompt for each: the task, your business context, and the format. Then improve it with follow-ups such as "shorter", "friendlier" or "give me three options".
Try the same prompt in two assistants and compare. You will quickly see which one fits your style. Free plans have limits that change; check the tool's own pricing page for what is included today.
Step by step:
- Open one assistant in a web browser or its official app.
- Write a three-part prompt for a real business job.
- Ask for one improvement.
- Paste the same prompt into a second assistant and compare.
Words to know:
- Free plan: a version of a tool you can use without paying, usually with limits.
Try it now: Write a prompt asking for a 50-word description of your business for a social media profile. Run it in two chat assistants. Keep the better one and note which tool you chose.
You can now choose a chat assistant that fits your accounts and use it for real business writing.

check.q: What is a fair way to compare two chat assistants?
options: Pick the one with the nicest logo
Ask a different question in each
Run the same prompt in both
check.why: The same prompt shows which tool answers your need better.

check.q: Your shop uses Outlook and Word every day. Which chat assistant do you try first?
options: One that needs a new account
A paid tool you have never heard of
check.why: A tool that fits the accounts you already use is a natural first choice.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Design with AI in Canva
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a simple branded graphic for your business with Canva.
This lesson builds toward: Using a Canva template, you will make a branded graphic with one message, one picture and one call to action, with every AI image checked for errors and copied logos before use.
Canva (canva.com) is a design tool with a free plan, thousands of templates and AI features that can suggest text, generate images and resize designs. You do not need design training to make a clean flyer or social post.
Start from a template, not a blank page. Search for what you need, such as "Instagram post bakery" or "flyer cleaning service". Change the words, swap in your colors and logo, and keep it simple: one message, one picture, one call to action.
If you use an AI-generated image, look closely for errors such as strange hands or misspelled words, and do not make an image that copies someone else's logo, brand or a real person without permission.
Step by step:
- Open canva.com and sign in or create a free account.
- Search for a template for the design you need.
- Change the text to your message and call to action.
- Add your colors and logo.
- Check spelling and images, then download.
Words to know:
- Template: a ready-made design you change to fit your business.
- Brand colors: the two or three colors you always use so customers recognize you.
Try it now: Make one social post or flyer for your business in Canva from a template. Use your business description from the last lesson and one call to action. Download it.
You can now make a clean, branded graphic in Canva and check AI images before you use them.

check.q: What is a call to action on a flyer?
options: A clear next step, such as "Text us to book"
check.why: A call to action tells people what to do next.

check.q: AI makes an image for you that looks like a famous brand's logo. What do you do?
options: Do not use it and make a different image
Shrink it so no one notices
check.why: You should not use images that copy another company's logo.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI in your daily business tools

lessons.title: Lesson 4: AI in documents and spreadsheets
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a document and to understand a spreadsheet.
This lesson builds toward: Given a simple sales sheet or document, you will use AI to write a spreadsheet formula and draft a document, testing the formula on rows checked by hand and sending legal documents for review.
Google Docs and Sheets and Microsoft Word and Excel now include AI helpers on many plans (Gemini in Google Workspace, Copilot in Microsoft 365). Which features you get depends on your plan, and that changes, so check the help pages for your account.
If your plan does not include the built-in helper, you can still use a free chat assistant: paste in text with no private details, or describe your columns, and ask for a draft, a formula or an explanation.
Useful asks: "Turn these notes into a one-page service agreement draft for my lawyer to review." "Write a spreadsheet formula that adds up column C when column B says Paid." "Explain what this formula does." Always test a formula on a few rows you can check by hand.
Step by step:
- Open a document or spreadsheet you already use.
- Look for the built-in AI helper; if there is none, open a chat assistant.
- Ask for a draft or a formula, describing your columns without private data.
- Test any formula on a few rows you can check yourself.
Words to know:
- Formula: an instruction in a spreadsheet cell that calculates something, like a total.
- Google Workspace / Microsoft 365: the paid business versions of Google's and Microsoft's office tools.
Official sources:
- Google Workspace: Gemini features
- Microsoft Support: Copilot
Try it now: Describe a simple sales sheet (date, item, amount, paid or not) to an AI assistant and ask for a formula that totals only the paid sales. Make a five-row test sheet and check the formula by hand.
You can now use AI to draft documents and write and test spreadsheet formulas.

options: An instruction in a cell that calculates something
check.why: Formulas calculate results from the data in your sheet.

check.q: You want AI to write a formula for your customer sales sheet. What do you share?
options: The full sheet with customer names
A description of the columns without private data
check.why: Describing the columns gets you the formula without sharing private data.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Meeting notes and transcription
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Turn a meeting or voice memo into clear notes and action items with AI.
This lesson builds toward: Given a meeting or voice memo, you will turn it into written notes and an action list with AI, with who, what and by when for each item, and permission before recording others.
Many tools can now turn speech into text: the voice recorder on many phones, the transcription features in Microsoft Teams, Google Meet and Zoom on some plans, and voice typing in Google Docs (Tools, then Voice typing) or dictation in Word.
Once you have the text, a chat assistant can turn it into a summary with decisions and action items: who does what by when. Remove private customer details before you paste.
Always tell people before you record or transcribe a call. Laws about recording calls differ by state and country, and some require everyone's consent, so asking first is the safe habit.
Step by step:
- Tell everyone you want to record or transcribe, and get a yes.
- Record or transcribe the meeting or a voice memo.
- Remove private details from the text.
- Ask AI: "Summarize this into decisions and action items: who, what, by when."
- Check the summary against what you remember.
Words to know:
- Action item: a task from a meeting with a person and a due date.
- Consent: permission given by a person before something is done.
Try it now: Record a two-minute voice memo about what your business must do this week. Transcribe it with voice typing or your phone, then ask an AI assistant to turn it into an action list with dates.
You can now turn spoken notes into a written action list, and ask permission before recording others.

check.q: What three things should each action item say?
options: The date, the weather and the topic
check.why: Who does what by when makes an action item clear.

check.q: You want to record a call with a supplier to make notes. What do you do first?
options: Tell them and ask their permission
Ask AI if it is allowed
check.why: Tell people and get permission before recording.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Building your toolkit and keeping it safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose one tool per job and set a safety rule for each.
This lesson builds toward: At the end of the course, you will create a one-page AI toolkit with one tool per job and a safety rule for each, listing something you made with each tool.
A toolkit you actually use beats a long list of apps you tried once. For each of the four jobs, pick one tool, note whether you are on a free or paid plan, and write one thing you made with it.
Check each tool's data settings. Many let you turn off chat history or stop your content being used to train the AI. Business plans often have stronger privacy terms; read the tool's privacy page before putting business documents in.
Set one simple rule per tool, such as "No customer phone numbers in ChatGPT" or "Only download Canva images I have checked". Review your toolkit every few months, because tools, features and prices change.
Step by step:
- List the four jobs.
- Pick one tool for each and note free or paid.
- Open each tool's settings and find its data or privacy options.
- Write one safety rule per tool.
- Put a reminder to review the toolkit in three months.
Words to know:
- Toolkit: the short list of tools you rely on, with what each is for.
- Privacy settings: options that control what a tool keeps and how it uses your data.
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page "My AI Toolkit": four jobs, one tool each, one thing you made with it in this course, and one safety rule for each tool.
You can now run your business with a small, safe AI toolkit that you review over time.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Four jobs covered A job is missing or two tools do the same job. Writing, design, documents or numbers, and meetings or notes, with one tool each. Says why each tool was chosen over another. Made with each tool One or more tools has nothing made with it. Lists one real thing made with each tool, such as a profile text, a flyer, a formula and an action list. The things made are already in use in the business. Checked results A formula, image or document was used without checking. Formula tested on rows checked by hand; images and documents checked before use. Notes which documents need a lawyer or professional review. Safety rules A tool has no safety rule, or a rule is vague. Each tool has one clear rule for customer data. Also notes the data setting changed in each tool and when to review the toolkit. Free plan and fit Free or paid is not stated, or the tool does not fit the business accounts. Free or paid noted for each tool, checked on its pricing page. Notes what a paid plan would add and whether it is worth it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a toolkit safety rule?
options: A rule such as "no customer phone numbers in AI chats"
check.why: A safety rule says how you protect data in each tool.

check.q: Six months after making your toolkit, a tool changes its free plan. What do you do?
options: Check the tool's own pricing page and update your toolkit
check.why: Tools and prices change, so you review the toolkit over time.
